title: Where Is Node.js Used?
learning_outcomes: Describe Web servers and REST APIs and explain how it relates to Where Is Node.js Used?.
Demonstrate Real-time applications in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Command-line tools.

content.intro: Where Is Node.js Used? is part of introduction to nodejs. This lesson connects Web servers and REST APIs, Real-time applications, Command-line tools to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: Web frameworks build on Node.js APIs; they provide routing and middleware but are not part of the Node.js runtime itself. Test routes, middleware order, invalid requests, not-found behavior, and centralized error responses.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Web frameworks build on Node.js APIs; they provide routing and middleware but are not part of the Node.js runtime itself. Keep route handlers focused, validate inputs, centralize async errors, and pin/document the framework version.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Where Is Node.js Used?. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Web servers and REST APIs; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Real-time applications, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Confusing framework behavior with core Node.js behavior or relying on middleware without verifying its order.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Read the framework guide for the selected major version and test route and middleware contracts.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
